Note that in these cases, the means of communication are somewhat 
old-fashioned: letters, telegraphs, and telegrams. Today phones, email, 
messaging and other forms of electronic media serve as the means by 
which offers are typically made; see, for example, International 
Casings 
Group, Inc. v. Premium 
Standard 
Farms, Inc., 358 F.Supp.2d 863 
(W.D.Mo.2005), in 
which the 
court 
examines 
a 
lengthy 
email 
correspondence between the parties. Yet the importance for purposes of 
contract formation is less the medium than the intent revealed by the 
communication; see Brighton Investment, 
Ltd. v. Har-ZVI, 
88 A.D.3d 
1220, 932 N.Y.S.2d 214 (2011) ("an exchange of emails may constitute an 
enforceable contract, 
even if a party 
subsequently 
fails to sign 
implementing documents, 
when the communications 
are "sufficiently 
clear and concrete" to establish such an intent").
